hints: Track where the first row goes after a clockwise turn: in the sample, 1 2 3 ends up as the last column read top to bottom. Can you get there with simpler moves you already know?

A clockwise turn equals a transpose (swap grid[i][j] with grid[j][i]) followed by reversing every row. Both steps work in place, so no second grid is needed — and the function returns nothing because grid itself is checked.

1. Let n = grid.length.
  2. For every i < j, swap grid[i][j] and grid[j][i] (transpose).
  3. For every row, swap from both ends towards the middle (reverse).
  4. Return nothing; grid now holds the answer.

approaches.name: Extra grid
approaches.idea: Build a new grid where res[j][n−1−i] = grid[i][j], then copy it back into grid.

approaches.name: Optimal (in place)
approaches.idea: Transpose the grid in place, then reverse each row in place.

explain: Transposing the sample gives rows 1 4 7, 2 5 8, 3 6 9. Reversing each row gives 7 4 1, 8 5 2, 9 6 3, which is what grid holds at the end. In the transpose loop only swap when j > i; swapping every pair would undo itself and leave the grid unchanged. Building a new array and assigning it to grid would not work, because the caller still looks at the original array.
recognize: "Rotate a square grid 90°, in place" → transpose + reverse each row.
